en: Verses on the Essential Dharma Spoken by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna for King Śāntaka.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśa during the Song Dynasty.
King Śāntaka, you should know that the suffering and affliction of birth and death involve manifold faults.
All are shrouded and obstructed by ignorance; I wish to bring them benefit.
Just as when an image of the Buddha is carved or painted, the wise who see it should show reverence;
so too, I rely on the Tathāgata to preach the True Dharma, and Your Majesty should likewise receive it with deep faith.
Although you have previously heard the words of the Muni, if you now listen and receive them with further discernment,
it will be like a lotus pond of pure color, where the moonlight shines down, surpassing the brilliance of the sun.
The Buddha taught that one should practice the six recollections, namely: the Three Jewels, generosity, ethical discipline, and the devas;
by practicing the ten wholesome paths of action, one purifies the three types of karma, remaining free from alcohol, negligence, and wrong livelihood.
Contemplate that body, life, and wealth are swiftly subject to decay; one should give to the field of merit to relieve the destitute.
Giving is a firm and steadfast bond beyond compare, the foremost among all forms of intimacy.
Diligently cultivate pure precepts to eliminate defilements, and do not harbor hopes or desires for the various realms of existence;
just as the great earth nurtures all things, so too do the precepts give birth to all virtues.
Cultivating patience, gentleness, and relinquishing anger—the Buddha says this practice is supreme;
likewise, through diligence, meditation, and wisdom—one who possesses these six practices transcends birth and death.
If one can be filial to one's parents while living at home, this is called the supreme field of merit;
in the present life, one’s great reputation will spread far and wide, and in the future, one’s karmic rewards will become immeasurable.
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, deception, and indulgence in wine;
Ornate beds that are high and wide, the use of perfumes, Singing, dancing, and performances, and eating at improper times— One should distance oneself from such manifold evils.
If one practices these precepts for even a short time, One will surely receive celestial bliss and ascend to Nirvana.
Avarice, envy, greed, and deceit, Deception, delusion, perversion, and indolence—
O Great King, you should contemplate these many evil and unwholesome dharmas And swiftly abandon them.
Physical beauty, nobility, and the five sensual pleasures—know them to be as precarious and decaying as bubbles or foam.
Do not rely on such unstable phenomena; arrogance, negligence, and self-indulgence give rise to all manner of suffering.
If you wish to increase all virtues and realize the nectar of immortality, you should distance yourself from them as you would cast away poison.
Those who are able to apply themselves with diligence and abandon anger and pride— like the autumn moon revealed when clouds are cleared away,
or like Aṅgulimāla and Nanda, and likewise like Kṣema and other noble ones.
The Tathāgata has taught three kinds of speech: that which enters the mind, the truth, and the false.
Speech that enters the mind is like a flower; the truth is like honey; falsehood is base and evil, like excrement and filth.
One should cultivate the first two types of speech and should swiftly sever the false.
There are four kinds of dharmas that lead from light into light; Your Majesty should discern and contemplate them with care.
You should practice the two types that lead into light, and if you encounter the darkness of delusion, you should swiftly abandon it.
The four transformations of the *āmra* fruit are such that it is difficult for people to distinguish them;
likewise, one should observe with profound wisdom and associate only with those who are truly virtuous and good.
Even if one sees a woman who is exceedingly beautiful and dignified, one should regard her as one’s own mother, elder sister, or daughter;
should a defiled mind of lustful desire arise, one ought to correctly practice the meditation on impurity.
This mind is restless and should be restrained, As one guards one's life or precious treasures;
If desire arises, one should be struck with fear, Just as one dreads swords, blades, or ferocious beasts.
Sensual desire is profitless like a poisonous enemy; such are the words spoken by the Muni.
The cycle of birth and death is a fault worse than the bonds of prison; one should diligently practice to seek liberation.
The six sense bases are restless, racing toward all objects; one should restrain them and not be negligent.
If one can thus control the faculties, it is superior to a valiant general who crushes a powerful enemy.
This body is impure, with nine orifices from which flows a stream that knows no end, like a river or the ocean;
though covered by thin skin as if it were pure, it is merely adorned with borrowed ornaments.
Only those who possess wisdom can discern this; knowing it to be empty and deceptive, they cast it aside.
Just as one with scabies approaches a fierce flame—though there is brief pleasure at first, it later increases the suffering—so too is the thought of sensual desire:
though there is initial attachment and delight, in the end it brings much affliction.
To see the true nature of the body as entirely impure is precisely to contemplate emptiness and non-self;
those who can cultivate this contemplation achieve the supreme among all benefits.
Though one possesses noble appearance, lineage, and great learning, if lacking precepts and wisdom, one is no different from birds and beasts;
though one dwells in an ugly or lowly station and has little learning or insight, if one can cultivate precepts and wisdom, one is called a superior person.
The eight worldly dharmas of gain and loss cannot be avoided by anyone, yet if one can eliminate and sever them, such a person is truly peerless.
Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas there may be— whether parents, wives, children,
or kinsmen— do not, out of consideration for them, accept their words and extensively perform unwholesome and unrighteous deeds;
even if one should commit various transgressions for their sake, the resulting great suffering in the future will be experienced by oneself alone.
Now, when one commits various evils that do not yield immediate retribution, it is not like swords and blades meeting in mutual wounding and slicing;
rather, at the moment of death, the signs of one's sins first all appear together, and thereafter one enters hell and undergoes manifold sufferings.
Faith, precepts, generosity, learning, wisdom, shame, and remorse—these seven dharmas are called the noble treasures.
The Muni has taught that they are truly incomparable, surpassing all the worldly jewels.
Great King, if you gather these supreme treasures, before long you too shall realize the fruit of the site of enlightenment.
Gambling, drinking to intoxication, and fondness for lutes and zithers; Laziness, arrogance, indolence, and evil companions;
Untimely actions, frivolity, and much restlessness— These seven things one should keep far away from.
Contentment is the supreme treasure, surpassing all other wealth; such are the words spoken by the World-Honored One.
Though one may be poor, if they are content, they may be called rich; to have wealth while harboring great desire is to be called poor.
If one’s accumulation of wealth increases various sufferings, it is like a dragon with many heads—the more heads, the more the venom increases.
One should contemplate delicious flavors as being like poison; purify them by sprinkling the water of wisdom.
Although one must eat to sustain this body, do not crave its color or taste to nourish pride and arrogance.
One should cultivate weariness toward all defiled desires and diligently seek the unsurpassed path to Nirvana.
Harmonize this body so that it is peaceful and secure; thereafter, you should practice the fast and precepts.
A single night is divided into five periods; during two of these periods, one should sleep and rest.
During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, contemplate birth and death; you should diligently seek liberation and not let the time pass in vain.
One should cultivate the four immeasurable concentrations; this is called opening the path to the Brahma realm.
If one focuses the mind single-mindedly on the four dhyānas, at the end of life one will surely be reborn in those celestial abodes.
All conditioned things are shifting and impermanent; they are suffering, empty, subject to decay, and lack solidity.
They are without self, without bliss, and impure—all such [teachings] are called the dharmas of remediation.
If there are those who deeply contemplate this dharma-gate, they shall forever occupy positions of honor and nobility in the future;
practicing the five precepts and severing the five perversions—this is what the Great King should also keep in mind.
Just as a small amount of salt placed in the Ganges cannot make the water salty,
so too, when subtle evil encounters a multitude of virtues, it is extinguished and dispersed.
If the five perversions increase, they will plunder one's merit; Your Majesty should eliminate them so that they do not grow.
The five faculties, such as faith, are the source of all virtues; these should be cultivated so that they flourish.
The eight sufferings, such as birth, are constantly ablaze; you should hold the water of wisdom and sprinkle it to extinguish them.
Those who seek celestial bliss and nirvana should diligently cultivate right knowledge and vision;
though one may possess sharp intelligence, if they enter a wrong path, subtle and wondrous virtues will never remain.
The four kinds of perversions harm all that is wholesome; therefore, one should contemplate them so they do not arise.
That is: form is not the self, the self is not in form; within the self there is no form, and in form there is no self.
These four types of mental states regarding form apply likewise to all the remaining aggregates.
These twenty states of mind are called perversions; if one can eliminate and sever them, that is supreme.
Phenomena do not arise of themselves, nor are they born from a primordial darkness; they are not created by Īśvara, nor do they exist spontaneously.
All arise from ignorance, craving, and karma; if causes and conditions are absent, they are severed and destroyed.
Since the Great King now knows these causes, he should kindle the lamp of wisdom to shatter the darkness of delusion;
for the view of a self, attachment to precepts and rituals, and the fetter of doubt—these three can obstruct the path to the outflow-free state.
If a king destroys and causes [the Dharma] to perish, the noble Dharma of liberation shall not be manifested;
it is like a blind man asking about the characteristics of water—he cannot comprehend them even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Seeking nirvāṇa is likewise: one must only exert oneself with diligence before realization is attained.
If one wishes to rely on kinsmen and acquaintances, those who can provide such support are exceedingly rare;
therefore, Great King, you should apply yourself with diligence, for only then can you realize cessation.
Generosity, morality, extensive learning, and meditative concentration—by means of these, one gradually approaches the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, O Lord of Men, you should cultivate the clarity of wisdom; by practicing these three dharmas, one seeks liberation.
If one can practice this Supreme Vehicle, then all other virtues will be encompassed.
Great King, you should contemplate the dharma of mindfulness of the body; the World-Honored One has declared this to be the path of purification.
If one lacks this mindfulness, unwholesome thoughts will increase; therefore, you ought to practice it with diligent effort.
Human life is brief and does not endure; it is like a bubble upon the water that arises and vanishes in an instant.
Between the exhalation and inhalation, and even amidst sleep, every thought-moment constantly departs and perpetually decays.
Before long, one shall witness its own destruction: the skin and flesh will rot and fester, becoming utterly loathsome.
Blue-black, bloated, and decaying, with pus and blood flowing; Worms and maggots devour it until it is exhausted;
Hair, body hair, nails, and teeth are scattered apart; Blown by the wind and scorched by the sun, they gradually dry up and vanish.
One should know that this body is not firm, but is an accumulation of immeasurable sufferings;
therefore, the noble ones and all wise people contemplate these faults and abandon it entirely.
Mount Sumeru, the great oceans, and the rivers—when seven suns shine upon them all at once, they melt away and dry up;
if even such firm and solid things can be destroyed, how much more so this fragile and precarious body?
When impermanence arrives, there is no refuge; it cannot be relied upon nor pursued.
Therefore, Great King, always observe this with clarity, and swiftly give rise to weary detachment to seek the Supreme Dharma.
A human body is difficult to obtain and the Dharma is difficult to hear, just like a blind turtle encountering a floating yoke with a single hole.
Having now attained such a rare body as this, one ought to listen to the True Dharma with a diligent mind;
to use this wondrous body to commit various evils is like using a precious vessel to hold a multitude of poisons.
Born in a central land and meeting virtuous friends, Diligently mindful, he resolved his mind and gave rise to right vows;
Having long cultivated merit and perfected all faculties, Your Majesty now fulfills this multitude of virtues.
Furthermore, associating with those who are seen and known [as noble ones], the Buddha has declared this to be the pure holy life (brahmacarya).
Therefore, one should joyfully follow it; by means of this, all Buddhas have realized nirvana.
Having encountered this subtle and pure Dharma, you should resolve to seek the path of detachment from desire.
The perils of birth and death are immeasurable in their suffering; though one were to proclaim them for an entire kalpa, they could never be fully exhausted.
Now, for the sake of the King, I shall briefly analyze them; you should listen attentively and reflect well.
The transformations within the three realms have no end; parents, wives, and children cause one another in succession.
Enemies and kin, hatred and love, dwell in no constant place; like a whirling firebrand, how could they ever reach an end?
Since beginningless time in the world of birth and death, the volume of mother’s milk one has drunk exceeds the waters of the great oceans;
if one does not diligently realize the wisdom of emptiness, one shall again drink it endlessly in the future.
Wandering through the five realms, passing through humans and devas, if one were to pile up the bones of these bodies, they would exceed Mount Sumeru in height;
if one were to calculate the tears shed from the sorrow of parting from loved ones, they could not be matched even by the great rivers;
and if one were to count the parents of a single person, they would surpass the number of plants and trees in the world.
Though one may enjoy the pleasures of the five desires in the heavens, In the end, one will still fall back into the suffering of the evil realms.
The lifespans of the various devas are exceedingly long; The entertainments therein are difficult to describe:
Singing, lutes, and dancing produce exquisite sounds, With plaintive tones harmonious and refined, most pure and far-reaching.
With wondrous forms and exquisite colors, most majestic and sublime, they surround and attend him in joyful play.
A hundred flavors of sumptuous delicacies are fully provided; whatever the mind desires for enjoyment arrives spontaneously.
Precious ponds, fragrant and pure, are ever full of water, their perimeters strewn and covered with various wonderful flowers.
Birds of diverse colors gather upon it, their mournful calls blending together as they emit distant sounds;
the devas sport and bathe within its waters, such delights as these are beyond description.
When merit is exhausted at the end of life, the five signs of decay appear; at that time, the arising of suffering exceeds one's former pleasures.
Therefore, although there may be celestial maidens for diversion, the wise, having seen this, give rise to revulsion.
Though one may dwell atop towers and pavilions of precious jewels, one will inevitably fall back into foul and impure places;
though one may roam through the Nanda Garden in the heavens, one will eventually return to the Forest of Swords;
though one may bathe in the Mandārava pools of the devas, one will ultimately fall into the Hell of the Ash River.
Though one may occupy the rank of a Universal Monarch, one returns as a servant driven by others' will;
though one enjoys the desire-free delights of Brahmā, one falls again into the blazing suffering of the Avīci Hell;
though one dwells in celestial palaces endowed with radiance, one later enters the pitch-black darkness of hell.
What are called the Black Rope, Reviving, Burning, Cutting, Flaying, Piercing, and the Uninterrupted hells—these eight hells are perpetually ablaze;
they are all the retribution for the evil karma of sentient beings.
Some undergo great suffering like oil being pressed out; some have their bodies crushed like fine dust;
some have their limbs and joints severed and now scattered; some are further flayed, split, burned, and boiled;
some have boiling copper poured into their mouths; and some have their forms split apart by iron presses.
Iron dogs compete to devour them, while iron birds gather to peck and tear;
various kinds of venomous insects all bite and gnaw. Some are impaled upon glowing copper pillars as fierce, raging fires burn everything through;
due to the causes and conditions of their own sinful karma, there is no escape.
The boiling cauldrons surge up to the heights, Into which the inverted sinners are cast.
Human life is precarious and decays with extreme rapidity; It is like but a single breath of the gods.
If, within this brief lifespan, A person hears of these aforementioned sufferings yet feels no alarm or dread—
One should know that this mind is exceedingly firm, like a vajra, difficult to destroy. Whether seeing it depicted in a painting,
hearing of it from another, following the accounts in scriptures, or recollecting it by oneself—
when one knows such [suffering] is already difficult to endure, how much more so when it is experienced by one’s own body!
In the Avīci Hell, the Great Hell without interval or rescue, the various sufferings therein are inexhaustible.
Even if someone were to have their body pierced by three hundred spears for a single day,
compared to a single moment of suffering in the Avīci Hell, it would not equal even one-hundred-thousand-millionth part of it.
One must endure this great suffering for the duration of an eon, only after the conditions of one’s sinful karma are exhausted can one be released.
From whom do such afflictions arise? They all originate from the unwholesome actions of the three karmas.
Great King, although you currently have no such misfortune, if you do not cultivate the causes and conditions, you will fall.
Among the animals, suffering is immeasurable: some are bound and beaten;
because they lack faith, precepts, and learning, they constantly harbor evil intentions and devour one another;
for the sake of bright pearls, feathers, horns, tusks, bones, fur, hides, or flesh, they bring about mutual destruction and harm.
As a human being, one lacks mastery over one’s own carriage and constantly suffers the pain of tiles, stones, blades, and staves.
The suffering in the realm of hungry ghosts is likewise: whatever they desire is not obtained as they wish;
they are oppressed by hunger and thirst, distressed by cold and heat, and their sufferings such as exhaustion are truly immeasurable.
Their bellies are as vast as mountains, yet their throats are like needles; they cannot describe the excrement, urine, pus, and blood [within].
Naked and with disheveled hair, they are most hideous, like *tāla* trees scorched and lopped off;
at night, great fires blaze from their mouths, and various insects vie to swarm there and devour them.
Excrement, urine, feces, and various impurities—these cannot be obtained even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas;
even if one were to seek and find a small portion, they would soon be plundered by one another and lost.
The cool autumn moon brings the affliction of scorching heat; the mild spring days turn into bitter cold.
If one approaches the gardens, the various fruits are all gone; even if one reaches the clear streams, they have turned to parched dryness.
Due to the causes and conditions of sinful karma, one's lifespan is exceedingly long, lasting for fifteen thousand years.
Enduring manifold torments without respite, all these are the retributions of hungry ghosts;
the Perfectly Awakened One has explained the cause of such suffering as the karma of stinginess, greed, and envy.
If one's heavenly merit is exhausted but residual goodness remains, one may thereby become a king among men;
yet if one later becomes indolent and that merit is entirely spent, one will surely fall into the three evil realms without a doubt.
Some are born as asuras and give rise to arrogance; with anger, envy, greed, and malice, they increase all manner of afflictions.
Although the devas possess roots of goodness and virtuous conduct, because of their stinginess and envy, they lose their benefit and joy.
Therefore, one should know that the fetter of jealousy is a deeply evil dharma and should be abandoned.
Great King, you now fully understand that the faults of birth and death involve manifold sufferings;
you should diligently cultivate the virtues that transcend the world, as one who thirsts longs for a drink or as one whose head is ablaze seeks relief.
If you exert even greater diligence to sever all modes of existence, this will be the most supreme among all virtues.
One should diligently uphold the precepts and practice meditative wisdom, taming the mind to seek nirvāṇa.

Nirvāṇa is subtle and wondrous, transcending all marks; it is free from birth, old age, death, and decay and affliction, and likewise lacks mountains, rivers, the sun, and the moon. Therefore, one should swiftly realize and know it.
If you wish to realize the teacherless wisdom, you should single-mindedly cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment;
if one boards the ship of these factors of awakening, it is easy to cross over the great ocean of birth and death.
Regarding the fourteen matters that the Buddha did not explain, simply give rise to faith and do not harbor doubt;
you should only maintain a correct mind and apply yourself with diligent effort, resolutely cultivating all wholesome dharmas.
Ignorance conditions volitional formations, which condition consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, and becoming;
from becoming arises birth, and from birth arise old age and death.
If the causes and conditions of birth and death are exhausted and extinguished, one who thus correctly contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination is a person who beholds the Noble Lion.
If you wish to see the Four Truths in their proper sequence, You should diligently cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path.
Though one may dwell in honor and amidst the five desires, One may still attain the Noble Path and sever all fetters.
This fruit cannot be sought from another; It must be realized through the union of one's own mind.
I have spoken of all sufferings and of Nirvāṇa for the sake of benefiting and refreshing you, Great King;
you should not give rise to a mind of fear. Rather, diligently recite, study, and practice all that is wholesome.
The mind is the root of all phenomena; if it is first tamed, all tasks will be accomplished.
I have briefly analyzed the essentials of the Dharma; Your Majesty should not yet feel satisfied.
If there is one of great wisdom who further expounds it, you should likewise listen with a sincere and diligent mind.
Your Majesty is now known as a great vessel of the Dharma; if you hear the teachings extensively, there will surely be much benefit.
If you see others practicing the goodness of the three karmas, you should deeply assist them and give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
Whatever good you yourself practice, along with that sympathetic joy—may all such merit be dedicated [for the welfare of all].
The King should look up to and emulate the various worthy sages, such as Avalokiteśvara and others who deliver sentient beings;
in the future, he will surely attain perfect enlightenment, and his kingdom shall be free from birth, old age, and the afflictions of the three poisons.
Great King, if you cultivate these supreme virtues, Then your beautiful reputation will spread far and wide;
Thereafter, using this to transform others, You shall cause all beings everywhere to attain perfect enlightenment.
The swift river of afflictions sweeps away sentient beings;
for the sake of extinguishing such defilements—the source of profound terror and blazing suffering—one should cultivate the truth of genuine liberation.
By departing from all worldly dharmas of provisional names, one attains the pure and immovable state.
If there is a woman harboring a harmful heart, such a wife should be avoided from afar;
but if she is chaste, harmonious, and loves her husband with respect, humble and diligent in her duties like a servant,
always regarded as a close friend, a sister, or a mother— she should be honored and respected like the tutelary deity of the household.
The Dharma I have taught is exactly thus; O King, you should practice it diligently day and night.
These verses on the essentials of the Dharma were spoken by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna for King Caṇḍaka.
